messages.author: 4e9f2d72eb0a8b62
messages.subject: Multiple datasets with rstan
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to simulate multiple datasets (say 100) and to run stan on each of them (each with 1 chain), to estimate the posterior of a parameter, VE from each of the dataset.

I came across a thread on similar topic and used similar command other users have suggested to do the above. 

Here is what it looks like:


fit.est <- stan(file = "2016_07_06_tnd_misclass.stan", data = sdata.list[[1]], init = "random", chains = 1) # compile code

chains <- 100

model.fit <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) {
  stan(fit = fit.est, data = sdata.list[[chain]], chains = 1, verbose = TRUE, warmup = 1000, refresh = -1, iter = 4000, chain_id = chain, seed = 12345, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9, max_treedepth = 15))
}) # update empty object in sim number of way


Can anyone please advise if my command is alright? I have got some results, but quite confident about it.

Also, in my case, as my aim is to estimate posterior from each dataset, do I still need run sflist2stanfit?

Thanks much for advice.

Huiying

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Multiple datasets with rstan
parts:
On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 1:42:39 AM UTC-4, huiying wrote:
model.fit <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) {
  stan(fit = fit.est, data = sdata.list[[chain]], chains = 1, verbose = TRUE, warmup = 1000, refresh = -1, iter = 4000, chain_id = chain, seed = 12345, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9, max_treedepth = 15))
}) # update empty object in sim number of way


Can anyone please advise if my command is alright? I have got some results, but quite confident about it.
You probably want to include mc.cores = parallel::detectCores() and mc.preschedule = FALSE in the call to mclapply(). You will have to see what value of adapt_delta is necessary for these models.
Also, in my case, as my aim is to estimate posterior from each dataset, do I still need run sflist2stanfit?

No, since sflist2stanfit() is intended for the typical situation where you are conditioning on the same data for all of the chains.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Multiple datasets with rstan
parts:
Do you have uncertainty in the prevalence and sensitivity
estimates?

Just some comments on efficiency.

This:

for (iin in 1:N)
obs_flu[iin] ~ binomial(1, p[iin]); // Binomial likelihood of an observed positive flu testAnother one for our list of flags.

should be coded as

obs_flu ~ bernoulli(p);

You don't ever want to use a binomial with total
count of 1 as it reduces to a Bernoulli.

I can't understand this

for (iin in 1:N)
p[iin] <- ((1 - delay[iin]) * ((1 - vaccine[iin]) * pi0 + vaccine[iin] * pi0 * (1 - VE)) + delay[iin] * ((1 - vaccine[iin]) * pi1 + vaccine[iin] * pi1 * (1 - VE))) * ((1 - delay[iin]) * sens0 + delay[iin] * sens1);

It could be vectorized, or you could break it down into the
16 underlying cases based on all those 0/1 indicators---multiplying
by 0 and 1 is very wasteful.

If the model's fast enough, the only thing I'd worry about is
trying to organize that iin loop. (We also recommend just
using for (n in 1:N) so the loop variable is the lower case
version of the size where possible to make programs easy to read.)

- Bob

That's sampling uncertainty, which is different (and also important).

> This:
>
> for (iin in 1:N)
> obs_flu[iin] ~ binomial(1, p[iin]); // Binomial likelihood of an observed positive flu testAnother one for our list of flags.
>
> should be coded as
>
> obs_flu ~ bernoulli(p);
>
> You don't ever want to use a binomial with total
> count of 1 as it reduces to a Bernoulli.
>
> Agree with that. Thanks ! but should I keep for (n in 1:N), because p for each observation is different?

No, it's vectorized, so when you write the above, it's
just a more efficient version of writing:
for (n in 1:N)
obs_flu[n] ~ bernoulli(p[n]);

>
> I can't understand this
>
> for (iin in 1:N)
> p[iin] <- ((1 - delay[iin]) * ((1 - vaccine[iin]) * pi0 + vaccine[iin] * pi0 * (1 - VE)) + delay[iin] * ((1 - vaccine[iin]) * pi1 + vaccine[iin] * pi1 * (1 - VE))) * ((1 - delay[iin]) * sens0 + delay[iin] * sens1);
>
> It could be vectorized, or you could break it down into the
> 16 underlying cases based on all those 0/1 indicators---multiplying
> by 0 and 1 is very wasteful.
>
> p is the probability of obs_flu ==1. It is written that way because it's value depends on whether delay/vaccine is 0 or 1 at each observations, and delay/vaccine are simulated randomly based on some pre-defined values using rbinom. Do you mean it's more efficient to calculate p separately based on different scenarios? How do I write that?

Let me give you a simple example.

You can write the Bernoulli pmf this way:

Bernoulli(y | theta) = theta^y * (1 - theta)^(1 - y)

or on the log scale

log Bernoulli(y | theta) = y * log(theta) + (1 - y) * log(1 - theta)

Either way, it's a lot more work than writing this:

Bernoulli(y | theta) = y == 0 ? theta : (1 - theta)

or on the log scale

log Bernoulli(y | theta) = log(y == 0 ? theta : (1 - theta))

or putting it in a conditional.

real bernoulli(real y, real theta)
if (y == 0)
return theta;
else
return 1 - theta;

The downside to having four boolean conditions is that you need
sixteen bodies to deal with all the cases if you want to do it within
the Stan program and don't want wasteful multiplications.

- Bob
